Aurora Project Manager · User Guide

Running a go-live in Aurora

How Harris Computer implementation teams plan, track, and report on customer projects — from your first login to closing out a monthly report. Screenshots throughout are from a sample TRIO environment; your projects and people will differ, but the screens work the same way.

How Aurora is organized

Four levels, from broadest to most granular.

Every implementation team at Harris Computer works out of one of five software lines — TRIO, MSI, Spectrum, OpenWindow, or ResourceMate. Your account belongs to exactly one home line, and everything you see in Aurora — projects, task boards, reports — is scoped to it. Admins can always switch which line they're looking at from the sidebar; Project Leads and Members can too, but only into lines an admin has explicitly granted them — see Users & access requests.

Inside a line, work breaks down like this:

Project A single customer engagement
"Lakeview Township — Payroll Go-Live"
→
Sub-project One product being delivered
"Data Conversion"
→
Task The actual work item
"Validate converted employee records"

Sub-projects come from two shared catalogs your admins maintain: Project Types (the category a project belongs to, like "Payroll Implementation" — used mainly for reporting) and Products (reusable pieces of work like "Data Conversion" or "Staff Training" that get added to a project as sub-projects). A product can carry its own set of standard tasks that auto-populate every time it's used, so a new go-live doesn't start from a blank checklist.

Signing in

Accounts are created by an admin, or requested from the login screen.

Once you're in, what you see is shaped by two things: your role and your software line. Both are set by an admin when your account is created (or when your access request is approved), and only an admin can change them afterward, from the Users page.

Forgot your password? Click Forgot password? on the login screen and enter your email — if it matches an active account, you'll get an emailed link to reset it, valid for 1 hour and usable once. The response looks the same either way, so this can't be used to check who has an account here. An admin can also reset anyone's password directly, from Users.

For security, Aurora signs you out automatically after 4 hours of inactivity — no clicking, typing, or scrolling in any open Aurora tab. You'll land back on the login screen with a note explaining why. Your open project, sub-project, and task tabs are remembered and reappear when you log back in (for up to a week). Anything you were typing but hadn't saved is lost, so save long comments before you step away. Using Aurora normally never triggers this, and an admin never needs to do anything.

Roles at a glance

Four roles, from full control to view-only.

Admin and Project Lead differ in one specific way: Project Leads can maintain the shared Project Type and Product catalogs, Members can't. Beyond that, both work identically — including editing or archiving any project in their line, not just ones they created themselves. Every edit and archive/unarchive is recorded in the audit trail (see Activity) so there's still a record of who changed what. Deleting a project outright remains admin-only, even for its creator. Project Leads can also remove a sub-project from any project in their line, which Members can only do on projects they created. Read Only is covered on its own further down, since it changes how every screen behaves rather than just what's in the sidebar.

Capability Admin Project Lead Member Read Only
View projects, tasks & activity in their line YesYesYesYes
Comment, upload attachments, log time on tasks YesYesYes—
Create a project or task YesYesYes—
Edit or archive a project Any projectAny projectAny project—
Remove a sub-project from a project Any projectAny projectProjects they created—
Delete a project outright Any project———
Maintain Project Types & Products YesYes——

The Dashboard

Your landing page — a snapshot of the whole line at a glance.

  • Stat tiles — total projects, tasks completed this week, and hours logged. Every tile is a link: click one to open a page listing exactly what it's counting, right down to the individual tasks or logged hours behind the number. There's deliberately no running open-tasks count here — at a whole-line level it doesn't say much on its own; see Reports for open-task counts broken down by person and project instead. Every section on this page — stat tiles included — can be resized or hidden; see Customizing your dashboard below.
  • Upcoming deadlines — sits right below the stat tiles now. A calendar of every open task's due date, defaulting to Week view. Switch to Month or Day, or step through with the arrows and Today. Tasks marked N/A drop off this calendar, since they no longer have a live deadline to track. Follow-ups — scheduled either from a task's Comments form or directly on a project (see Task detail and Inside a project) — show up here too, as a plain Follow up pill rather than a task title; click one to jump back to whatever it was scheduled on. A completed follow-up shows crossed out rather than disappearing, and Day view adds a Mark complete / Reopen button for whoever's allowed to use it.
  • Hours logged follows the calendar — the third stat tile isn't a fixed "this week" total. It always totals whatever period the calendar above is currently showing: switch the calendar to Month view and the tile becomes Logged this month; page the calendar back to last week and it re-totals for that week instead. Switch to Day view for a single day's total.
  • Project progress — every active project with a completion bar; archived projects don't appear here. Like Recent activity, it shows the 2 most recent projects by default, with a Show more / Show less toggle for the rest.
  • Recent activity — a running feed of what's happened across the line: tasks created, moved, assigned, commented on, or logged against. Also collapsed to 2 entries by default.
  • My tasks — everything currently assigned to you, regardless of project. Each entry shows as Project – Sub-project – Task, so you can tell at a glance which project and product a task belongs to without opening it.
  • My projects — projects assigned directly to you, the same idea as My tasks but at the project level. Empty until someone assigns you a project.
Email reminders

Aurora also emails you directly, so you don't have to keep checking the calendar: you're emailed the moment you're assigned a task (see Task detail), and from then on task assignees get a daily reminder for anything overdue or due today, while whoever scheduled a follow-up gets reminded on its date. An overdue task keeps reminding once a day until it's resolved — closed, reassigned, or its due date moved — rather than a single email you might miss.

Customizing your dashboard

Click Customize, top right, and every card on the dashboard gets a dark title bar. Drag a card by its title bar to move it anywhere — the other cards shuffle out of the way — and drag its bottom-right corner to make it wider, narrower, taller, or shorter. A card too small for its content scrolls inside itself. Click the ✕ on a card to hide it; hidden cards appear as + buttons at the top, and clicking one puts it back at the bottom. How many items a list card (Project progress, Recent activity, My tasks, My projects) shows before Show more follows its width. Moving and resizing needs a reasonably wide window; on a narrow one the cards simply stack in order.

Save keeps your changes (nothing is saved until you click it, and Cancel drops them); Reset to default puts every card back to its original size and place, all visible. This is entirely personal — customizing your dashboard never changes what anyone else sees on theirs.

Drilling into a stat tile

Total projects opens the Projects list; Completed this week opens the sortable table above; the hours-logged tile opens a table of the individual time entries behind that total, including who logged them and any note attached — titled and scoped to match whichever period the tile itself was showing (today, this week, or this month) when you clicked it.

Projects

Where a customer engagement lives, from kickoff to go-live.

Browsing & creating a project

Grid / List in the top-left switches how projects are laid out — Grid for a card per project with its description and progress bar, List for a compact, denser table that's easier to scan once you have more than a handful of projects. Your choice is remembered on this device the next time you visit.

Click New project to start one. A project needs a name and a Project Type; everything else — including who it's assigned to — is optional at creation and can be filled in later.

Starting from a contract. If you have the customer's signed contract as a PDF, click Upload contract at the top of the form. Aurora reads it (scanned pages are fine, up to 100 pages) and fills in a suggested name, description, project type, the products it covers, and a TeamSupport ticket # if one is written in it — plus the contract lines (the billable services, with their hours and amounts) so you can track hours against what was sold. Nothing is created until you review the form and click Create project, and the PDF itself isn't kept. If the button says contract reading isn't set up, ask an admin.

Working with more than one project at once

Open a project — or any sub-project or task inside it — and a tab for it appears in a bar above the page content. Open a second project and its tab joins the first, so you can jump between them with one click instead of navigating back through the Projects list each time. The tab bar shows up everywhere, not just on project pages, so it stays put while you check the Dashboard or Reports too.

A sub-project or task's tab isn't just a copy of its parent project's — it carries its own label naming both itself and the project it belongs to (e.g. "Migrate customer accounts · Millbrook County — Utility Billing"), and always returns you to that exact page rather than the project's overview. Switching between any mix of open projects, sub-projects, and tasks lands you back exactly where you were.

Click the × on a tab to close it. Closing a tab you're not currently viewing just removes it from the bar; closing the one you're on takes you to whichever tab is next, or back to the Projects list if it was the only one open. Your open tabs are remembered on this device, so they're still there the next time you sign in — until you log out, which clears them so the next person to use this device isn't looking at your open projects.

Inside a project

  • New sub-project adds another product to this project at any time.
  • Copy project — see Copying a project below.
  • Edit project opens an inline form for the name and description; the TeamSupport ticket number field next to the title saves as soon as you click away from it. Any Project Lead or Member can edit any project in their line, not just ones they created.
  • Set a TeamSupport ticket # and Aurora fetches that ticket's live status right underneath — a status badge and its subject line. See TeamSupport integration for what else this unlocks.
  • No ticket yet? Click Create TeamSupport ticket next to the ticket number field. Aurora creates the ticket for you and fills in the number, attaching the project's TeamSupport Customer if you've picked one. See TeamSupport integration.
  • Archive project hides it from the Dashboard, Calendar, and default Projects list without deleting anything — it still shows up in Reports and behind Show only archived projects on the Projects page (check it to see just the archived ones). Any Project Lead, Member, or admin sees this button; Read Only accounts are the only ones who don't.
  • Delete project is permanent, including every sub-project, task, comment, and attachment underneath it — so only admins can do it, even if you created the project yourself. Project Leads and Members only see Archive project; if a project truly needs to go, ask an admin.
  • Each sub-project card has its own Remove button — it deletes that sub-project and its tasks without touching the rest of the project. Admins, Project Leads, and the person who created the project see it; Members who didn't create the project don't.
  • Assign to, next to the title, sets who's on the hook for the project as a whole — useful when one person is handling the entire engagement instead of being assigned task by task. Purely informational (it doesn't touch any task's own assignee), and assigning someone adds them as a Member automatically if they weren't one already.
  • Members controls who can be assigned tasks on this project; add or remove people from the dropdown.
  • Attachments here are project-level files, separate from the attachments on individual tasks. Click a file's name to view it inline in a new tab; Download next to it forces a save instead, and Remove deletes it for good.
  • Follow-ups schedules a reminder on this project directly, without tying it to any specific task — pick a date and click Schedule follow-up; there's no limit on how many a project can have open at once. Mark complete crosses it out here and on the Dashboard calendar; Reopen undoes that. Only whoever scheduled it, or an admin, can do either — see Task detail for the other way to schedule a follow-up.

Contract lines — tracking the hours you sold

A project can carry a Contract lines table: one row for each billable services line in the customer's contract (training, installation, project management, data conversion, go-live...). Each row has a product, a category, a description, the hours sold (when the contract gives them), and the amount in dollars. License and maintenance lines aren't tracked — there's no time to log on them — and neither are lines at $0 or marked no charge.

  • From a contract. On the New project form, Upload contract reads the PDF and fills in the lines for you. A line like "Training - 10 Hours" becomes 10 hours of Training, and a line like "Installation, Implementation, Setup, Config, PM" is filed under Project Management. Check them over — use Edit or Remove on any row, or + Add line — because they're saved along with the project when you click Create project.
  • By hand. On any project, the Contract lines card has + Add line, Edit and Remove. Projects created before this existed start with none.
  • Conversion lines. A line labeled conversion usually has an amount but no hours, so Aurora works the hours out at $200 an hour — an $800 conversion line becomes 4 hours. This also fills in the hours when you add a new conversion line by hand and leave them blank.
  • Hours used and left. Hours are tracked only on lines that have hours; a line without them (a flat-fee project management line, say) just shows its amount. The top of the card totals hours sold, used and left across those lines, and each line has its own bar that fills as time is logged — amber when it's nearly used up and red when it's over. Hours you log on a task comment count against a line: Aurora looks at the task's sub-project (its product) and the task itself, so time logged on a Staff Training task in the Budgetary sub-project counts against Budgetary Training. The action type you pick helps when the task name doesn't say. If Aurora can't tell which line it is, the hours simply aren't tied to one — the comment form shows a Contract line dropdown once you've typed hours, so you can choose.
  • Collapsing the card. Click the Contract lines heading to show or hide the table of lines. The Hours sold, Hours used and Hours left tiles and their bar at the top stay in view either way, so you can see where the project stands without scrolling. Aurora remembers your choice on this device, and the table starts hidden.

Copying a project

Copy project duplicates the whole thing under a new name you choose — same project type and description; same members; same sub-projects; and every task's title, assignee, priority, and due date. Task status is deliberately not carried over — every copied task starts fresh at To Do (any N/A reason is cleared too), since a copy represents a new engagement that hasn't done any of that work yet. You become the copy's owner regardless of who owned the original.

The TeamSupport ticket # is the one thing that's deliberately left blank on the copy — it identifies one specific support ticket, and the copy is a separate engagement that hasn't been tied to a ticket of its own yet. Comments, attachments, and time entries never come along either — those belong to the original engagement's history, not a fresh copy of it. Copying doesn't change the original project in any way; think of it as a quick way to set up a new engagement that looks like one you've already run, without rebuilding it product by product.

The task board

New task opens a form for title, description, priority, assignee, and due date. Click any task's title to open its full detail page.

When the Aurora Calendar link is set up, a tick box Also add to the Aurora Calendar appears under the assignee and due date (on a new task and on the task page). It's optional: ticked, the task shows on the calendar on its due date, for that line. It follows the task — change the title, assignee or due date and the calendar updates; untick it, unassign the task or delete the task and it comes off. If the calendar can't be reached the task still saves, and you're told so.

Drag a task card up or down within its column to reorder it — useful for putting the next thing to work on at the top. The new order is saved immediately and everyone viewing the board sees it. Dragging only reorders within a column; to move a task to a different status, use its dropdown instead.

Marking a task N/A

Not every task turns out to apply — a customer might supply their own training materials, or a step might get skipped for a reason worth recording. For situations like that, N/A sits alongside To Do, In Progress, and Done in the status dropdown, both on the task board and on a task's own detail page.

Choosing N/A prompts you for a short reason before the change goes through — it's required, so an N/A task always comes with an explanation attached. Cancel the prompt, or leave it blank, and the status stays exactly where it was. Once set, the reason shows in italics on the task's card and in its Details panel, visible to everyone who can see the task, including Read Only accounts.

N/A is deliberately its own bucket, not a variant of Done or a hidden version of open: it's excluded from open-task counts and overdue calculations everywhere in Aurora — the Dashboard, Upcoming deadlines, and Reports — and gets its own column so it can still be tracked and reported on separately.

N/A tasks also don't count toward progress percentages. If a sub-project has five tasks and you mark one N/A, the other four are worth 25% each, so finishing all four reads 100% instead of stalling at 80%. This applies to the progress bars and task counts on project cards, sub-project cards, and the Dashboard.

Task detail

  • Description is free text, editable inline.
  • Comments are a timestamped thread. Filling in Hours (and Date, if it isn't today) before you post also logs that time against the task — one form covers both, so a quick "did this, took 2 hours" update takes a single post. Leave Hours blank to just add a comment. Comments and Time entries each show the 3 most recent by default, with Show more / Show less to see the rest.
  • Follow-up date puts a Follow up reminder on the Dashboard calendar, assigned to whoever posts the comment. It's separate from the task's own due date and doesn't create a new task — clicking the reminder on the calendar takes you straight back to this task. See The Dashboard for where it shows up. A follow-up can also be scheduled directly on a project instead, without tying it to a task — see Inside a project. Either way, whoever scheduled it (or an admin) can mark it complete once it's done, which crosses it out wherever it shows up rather than removing it.
  • Action type and Visibility only appear when the task's project has a TeamSupport ticket # set — see TeamSupport integration for what they control. When they appear, Action type and Hours become required, marked with a small red * required, so a comment can't be posted without them.
  • Links and files in comments: a web address typed or pasted into a comment (starting with https://, http:// or www.) becomes a clickable link. Click Attach files under the comment box to add up to 10 files (25 MB each) to the comment; they show under it once it's posted, and also appear in the task's Attachments list. On a project with a TeamSupport ticket # set, the links and the files go to the ticket's note too.
  • Pictures: paste a screenshot straight into the comment box (or drag a picture onto it) and it's added to the comment with a small preview. Once posted, pictures show as thumbnails under the comment — click one to see it full size. In TeamSupport, pictures up to 2 MB also appear inside the note itself, as well as being attached as files; bigger ones arrive as attachments only.
  • Each comment carries its own Remove link, for people who can write to the task. Deleting a comment also removes any hours logged with it, but only in Aurora — it never reaches back into TeamSupport to undo a note that already synced there.
  • Attachments here belong to this task specifically. Click a file's name to view it inline in a new tab; Download saves it instead, and Remove deletes it.
  • Details — status, priority, assignee, and due date all live here. Status and Priority still save the instant you change them; switching status to N/A adds an N/A reason field right below it, showing the note you entered. Assignee and Due date are different: changing either one reveals Save and Cancel buttons instead of saving right away — nothing takes effect (and no one gets emailed) until you click Save. A task can't be saved with a real assignee and no due date, same rule as creating one; Due date is marked * required the moment you pick someone. Cancel discards whatever you changed and puts both fields back to what's actually saved. Once saved, the new assignee gets an email with the task and its due date — see The Dashboard for the other email reminders Aurora sends.
  • Delete task, top right, removes it along with its comments, attachments, and time entries.

If the task's project has a TeamSupport ticket # set, every comment and logged time posted here is mirrored to that ticket automatically — see TeamSupport integration below.

TeamSupport integration

Optional — only does anything once an admin configures an org ID and API token for your environment.

Setting a TeamSupport ticket # on a project (see Inside a project) links it to the matching support ticket. Once it's set, Aurora shows that ticket's live status and subject line right underneath the ticket number field — no need to leave Aurora to check where things stand. There's no link into the ticket itself here — TeamSupport doesn't support linking straight to one, so pull it up over in TeamSupport the way you normally would if you need to.

If a project doesn't have a ticket yet, click Create TeamSupport ticket next to the ticket number field (Read Only accounts don't see it). A small panel opens where you can pick the ticket's Product and Nature (both optional, and for some environments the Group and Ticket type too — see below); click Create ticket there and Aurora creates the ticket in TeamSupport and fills in the ticket # for you. The ticket's title is the project name, and its description is the project description plus a line saying who created it. Its severity is Normal, and it starts in the ticket type's first open status (Not Started for PS Projects tickets). If the ticket is created but its description or customer can't be added, Aurora tells you so and keeps the ticket linked.

Group and Ticket type: four environments have a fixed answer, and the panel just shows it: TRIO tickets go to the TRIO Support group, Spectrum tickets to Spectrum PS, MSI tickets to MSI PS, and OpenWindow tickets to OpenWindow PS — all as PS Projects tickets. In every other environment the panel has Group and Ticket type dropdowns (both required, listing TeamSupport's own groups and ticket types) and the Create button stays off until you've picked both. Product: start typing to search every TeamSupport product, or open the box empty to see your environment's own products (in TRIO, the ones named "TRIO …") first. Nature: choose from the list of options TeamSupport uses on these tickets. That list is kept inside Aurora, so if TeamSupport gets a new Nature option it won't appear here until Aurora is updated, but you can always change it in TeamSupport.

Projects have a searchable TeamSupport Customer field, on the project page and on the New project form. Start typing a customer's name and pick it from the list (choose No customer to clear it). When Aurora creates a ticket, it attaches that customer to the ticket. Pick the customer first: setting or changing it afterward doesn't change a ticket that already exists, so add it in TeamSupport for those. The customer list comes from TeamSupport and refreshes every few hours, so a brand-new customer can take a while to show up. Duplicating a project keeps its customer.

The same button is on the New project form, under the ticket # field. Fill in at least the project name first (it becomes the ticket's title); the description is used too. The new ticket's number drops into the field. The ticket is created the moment you click Create ticket in the panel, so if you then close the form without creating the project, the ticket stays in TeamSupport and has to be deleted there.

From there, every comment posted on any task in that project — with or without logged time attached — is also added to the linked ticket as a note, headed "Via [Software line] Project Manager" (e.g. "Via TRIO Project Manager"), followed by a line naming the sub-project and task the update came from (e.g. "Data Conversion — Validate converted employee records"), then the comment text itself; any logged hours ride along in the ticket's own time-tracking field rather than as extra text. Web addresses in the comment arrive as clickable links, any files attached to the comment are attached to the note, and pictures up to 2 MB also appear inside the note's text. This happens automatically; there's nothing extra to click. If TeamSupport is slow, unreachable, or not configured, your comment still saves in Aurora normally — the sync fails quietly in the background rather than blocking your update.

Once a project's ticket # is set, two extra fields appear on the comment form for every task in it: Action type, one of TeamSupport's standard "PS - …" categories (Training, Go Live, Support, and so on), and Visibility, which posts the synced note as either a Private or Public action in TeamSupport. Both Hours and Action type become required in this case — Aurora won't post the comment without them — since TeamSupport expects every note on a linked ticket to carry real time and a real category.

By default, every synced note is attributed in TeamSupport to whichever account owns the shared API token, not the actual Aurora user who wrote it. To fix that, an admin can link each Aurora account to its matching TeamSupport user from Users — a type-ahead field next to each person searches TeamSupport's user list by name as you type, so you can pick the right match without scrolling a long list. Once linked, that person's own comments and time logs show up in TeamSupport under their own name instead.

Read Only accounts

Full visibility, zero risk of an accidental change.

A Read Only account is meant for stakeholders who need to follow a project's progress — a customer contact, an internal sponsor — without being able to alter anything. It's not a stripped-down role so much as a mirror of the full app with every write action removed: no new projects, sub-projects, or tasks; no editing, commenting, uploading, or logging time; no status, priority, assignee, or due-date changes. Everything that would normally be a button, dropdown, or form is instead plain text.

Same task, same data — the sidebar loses everything but Dashboard, Projects, and Settings, and the details panel becomes read-only text. A Read Only user can still change their own theme, language, and password from Settings; that's the one place the role doesn't apply, since it's personal, not project, data.

Reports Admin only

Where progress across the whole line becomes numbers.

Five tabs cover the same underlying data from different angles:

  • By user — one row per person, with every project they touch listed alongside, plus any projects assigned directly to them.
  • By project — the same statistics rolled up per project (including who it's assigned to, if anyone) and again per project type.
  • Overdue tasks — a flat list of individual tasks that are either still open past their due date, or were completed after it. Nothing here is aggregated; it's meant for triage.
  • Activity — the full audit trail; see below.
  • Saved reports — build exactly the report you want: pick columns, filter, sort, run it (with CSV export) without even saving, or save it under a name to reuse later and share with every admin in the line. See below.

Filters sit above every tab:

  • Filter by user narrows every tab to one person — By Project and By Project Type switch from team-wide totals to just that person's own tasks and hours within each project, and Activity shows only what that person did.
  • From / To restricts completed tasks and logged hours to a date range on the first three tabs (open and overdue counts are deliberately left alone, since they describe the present, not a period); on the Activity tab it instead filters by when each entry happened.

Every By User / By Project / By Project Type table carries its own N/A column, counting tasks marked N/A separately from Open Tasks. Because N/A tasks are excluded from open and overdue math everywhere, marking a task N/A never inflates someone's overdue count or drags down their on-time rate — it just moves that task into its own bucket. The Overdue tasks tab never lists an N/A task either, even one whose due date has passed.

Every table has its own Export CSV button, producing exactly the rows on screen.

Saved reports

Click + New report to start one. Check off which columns to show — title, project, sub-project, assignee, status, priority, due date, completed date, days late, N/A reason, created by/at, hours logged — then narrow the results with any combination of status, priority, assignee, project, project type, a due-date or completed-date range, or a single Overdue only checkbox, and pick what to sort by.

Run report shows the results immediately, with the same Export CSV button every other report table has — you never have to save a report just to see or export it. Give it a name (and an optional description) and click Save report only once you want to reuse it: it then shows up in this list for every admin in the line to view and run, though only you can edit or delete it.

Activity — the audit trail

On top of the shared user and date filters, Activity adds a Type dropdown to narrow the list down to one kind of action — useful for, say, pulling up every status change on a project without wading through comments and attachments. The list is capped at 1,000 rows; if a filter combination still hits that cap, a notice above the table says so and suggests narrowing further, rather than silently leaving anything out.

Jarvis, the built-in helper

Ask a question in plain English and get an answer from your own project data.

The Ask Jarvis button in the left menu, just above your name, opens a small chat in the bottom-right corner. Type a question, or tap one of the suggestions, and Jarvis looks the answer up in Aurora for you. It is open to every role, including Read Only.

Things you can ask:

  • What's overdue? — open tasks past their due date, with the project, due date, and assignee.
  • Which projects are behind? — progress and overdue counts for each project in your line.
  • What's due this week? or What's assigned to Priya? — tasks filtered by date or person.
  • How many hours were logged this week? — totals, broken down by project and by person.
  • Catch me up on Lakeview Township — a short summary of one project.
  • What follow-ups do I have coming up? — your own open follow-up reminders.

Talking instead of typing: click the microphone button next to Send, say your question, and Jarvis sends it when you stop talking. Turn on the speaker button (🔊) at the top of the chat and Jarvis reads each answer aloud; a Voice menu appears so you can pick which voice it uses (Edge has especially natural ones), and your choice is remembered on that device. Both work in Chrome and Edge and follow your Aurora language; your browser asks permission to use the microphone the first time. The browser, not Aurora, turns your voice into text, which means the audio goes to the browser's maker (Google for Chrome, Microsoft for Edge). Typing always works.

New chat clears the conversation and starts over. Within one chat you can ask follow-up questions, such as "and which of those are Priya's?", and Jarvis remembers what you were just discussing.

What Jarvis can and can't do

Jarvis only reads — it can't create, change, or delete anything. It sees the same software line you're currently viewing (use the dropdown at the top of the sidebar to switch), and nothing from other lines. Your questions and the Aurora data needed to answer them are sent to an AI service to write the reply, and Aurora itself doesn't save your chats. Jarvis can be wrong, so double-check anything important in the project itself. Each person gets a daily limit on questions; if you reach it, it resets the next day.

Settings

Personal preferences — available to every role, including Read Only.

  • Theme — System follows your device; Light and Dark override it.
  • Accent color — six options, used throughout the interface for primary buttons and highlights.
  • Language — English, Spanish, or French (Canadian); switches immediately on save.
  • Change password — anyone can set their own, any time, no admin required.

Admin tools

Project Types and Products are also open to Project Leads; Users is Admin-only.

Users & access requests

  • Add user creates an account by hand, without going through an access request. Leave Email them an invite to pick their own password ticked and they get an email with a one-time link (works for 7 days) to choose their own password, so you never have to make one up. Untick it to type a starting password instead.
  • Email invite on a user's row sends them a fresh invite link — use it if the first one expired or got lost.
  • Filter by software line narrows the table to just one line — useful once you're managing users across several; defaults to All software lines.
  • Role and Software line are both editable inline, per user — changing a line doesn't move their existing project memberships or task assignments, so reassign deliberately.
  • Extra lines, for Project Leads and Members only, grants access to additional software lines beyond their home one. Click Manage lines to check off which ones; they'll see a line switcher appear in their own sidebar, and can move between their home line and every granted one with the same role-based permissions they already have — a Project Lead granted a second line is a Project Lead there too. Admins never need this (already unrestricted); Read Only accounts can't be granted extra lines at all.
  • Access request emails, for Admins only, controls which software lines' access requests each admin gets emailed about — click Manage notifications to open it. Every admin starts on Notify for every software line, so nothing changes until you deliberately narrow someone down; turn that off to reveal a checklist of specific lines instead. Turning it back on doesn't clear whatever lines were checked — they're just set aside, so switching it off again picks up right where you left it.
  • TeamSupport user is a type-ahead field — type a few letters of a name and matches pop up beneath it; click one to link the account, or click Not linked to clear it. See TeamSupport integration for what this changes.
  • Deactivate blocks sign-in without losing history; Delete removes the account entirely.

Project types & products

Deactivate on either page hides an item from new-project and new-sub-project pickers without touching anything already built from it. Both pages also carry a Delete action for items that were never meant to stick around. Each standard to-do task under Manage tasks has its own Edit and Delete too — Edit opens its title, description, and priority in an inline form, the same way editing a product itself works. Neither one reaches back into projects that already picked up a copy of that task: editing only changes the template for tasks created from it going forward, and deleting only stops it from being added to new projects.

Every product comes with a standard Project Management task, so there's always a place to log project management time. It's added automatically to new products and has been added to the existing ones; it works like any other standard task, so you can edit or delete it. Projects that already existed keep the tasks they have — it appears on projects created from now on.

Drag a standard to-do task up or down within the Manage tasks list to reorder it. This order is exactly what's used every time that product's tasks auto-create on a project — first template becomes the first task, and so on — so getting it right here means every future use of the product comes in correctly ordered, on the sub-project's task board, without having to reorder each one by hand afterward.

Switching software lines

The dropdown at the top of the sidebar swaps which line you're currently viewing across the entire app: Dashboard, Projects, Reports, Project Types, and Products all follow it. Admins always see every line there; Project Leads and Members see it too, but only once an admin has granted them at least one line beyond their home one (see Users & access requests) — otherwise the sidebar just shows their one home line as plain text, same as Read Only accounts always do.

This switch only lasts for your current session. Every time you log back in, Aurora resets you to your home line — the one set on your account in Users — regardless of which line you were last viewing before you logged out. If you spend most of your time in one particular line, make sure that's set as your home line so it's what you land on after every login.

Glossary

The handful of terms Aurora uses a specific way.

Software lineOne of five product lines — TRIO, MSI, Spectrum, OpenWindow, ResourceMate. Scopes everything below it.
ProjectA single customer engagement, e.g. a specific municipality's go-live.
Project assigneeWhoever's on the hook for a project as a whole, set from the project page — separate from a task's own assignee, and from simply being a project Member (though assigning someone adds them as a Member automatically).
Project typeThe category a project belongs to (e.g. "Payroll Implementation"), used for grouping and reporting.
ProductA reusable unit of work in the shared catalog (e.g. "Data Conversion") that becomes a sub-project when added to a project.
Sub-projectOne product as it exists inside a specific project — holds that product's tasks.
TaskThe actual to-do item: has a status, priority, assignee, due date, comments, attachments, and time entries.
N/A statusA task status for work that doesn't apply. Requires a reason, shows it to everyone, and is tracked separately from open and overdue counts.
TeamSupport ticket #Links a project to its TeamSupport ticket — shows that ticket's live status on the project page, and mirrors task comments and logged time there as notes. See TeamSupport integration.
TeamSupport user linkMaps an Aurora account to its matching TeamSupport user (Admin > Users) so notes synced from that account attribute to the right person instead of the shared API account.
Action type / VisibilityFields on a task comment, shown only when the project has a TeamSupport ticket # set — pick the "PS - …" category and Public/Private status for the note it syncs to TeamSupport.
Follow-upA reminder for a specific date, scheduled either from a task's comment form or directly on a project. Shows on the Dashboard calendar as a "Follow up" pill linking back to whichever it was scheduled on — it isn't a task itself, so it never appears in task counts or reports. Whoever scheduled it (or an admin) can mark it complete, which crosses it out rather than removing it.
Saved reportA named, reusable report built in Reports > Saved reports — its columns, filters, and sort are stored so it can be run again later. Visible to every admin in the line; only its creator can edit or delete it.
Built for Harris Computer implementation teams. If something in Aurora doesn't match what's described here, the app is the source of truth — let your admin know so this guide can catch up.
